newsitem.title: UK: Britons seek fixed mortgages as rate rise shield.
newsitem.headline: Britons seek fixed mortgages as rate rise shield.

text.p: Canny Britons are increasingly rejecting the volatility of the traditional variable rate mortgage and are instead opting for the security offered by products which fix the rate for the first few years, mortgage lenders say.

"Demand for fixed rate mortgages has increased significantly in the last six months in the climate of rising interest rates and as the prices offered have come down closer to the standard rate," said David Nicholson, head of mortgage marketing at Halifax PLC, Britain's largest mortgage provider.

The scurry for fixed rate home loans which do not move at the whim of changes in Britain's official interest rate has been sparked by three 1/4 point official rate rises in as many months and talk of more to come.

By historical standards both Britain's official interest rate at 6.75 percent and 8.2 percent standard mortgage rate are still low but the rising trend has triggered memories of the late 1980s when mortgage rates soared to more than 15.0 percent as the government increased official rates to dampen demand.

"The rationale for borrowers looking for fixed rate mortgages is to try and head off any increase in variable rates they would otherwise be liable to," said David Dooks, assistant director at the British Bankers' Association's (BBA) statistics division.
"There is a general expectation that base rates and therefore mortgage rates are going up and so fixed rates are looking very attractive," he said.

The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee will meet to discuss interest rates on August 6 and 7 and there is speculation that it could raise official interest rates to 7.0 percent from their current level of 6.75 percent as part of the attempt to prevent the exuberant consumer sector from pushing the economy into an unsustainable boom.
Fixed rate mortgages are a relative newcomer to the UK, having become widely available only in the current decade and there are therefore no comparable figures from the boom years of the 1980s.
But data from British mortgage lenders shows many homeowners are determined to avoid such punitive borrowing rates this time round.
The BBA said on Monday that 45 percent of all gross mortgage lending in the second quarter was at a rate fixed for some period of time, although it had no breakdown of the duration of the fixing.

The second quarter 1997 level was the highest since late 1993/early 1994 when interest rate jitters were also prevalent and the fixed rate proportion of gross lending was at its highest level at more than 60 percent.
By contrast in the first quarter of 1997 fixed rate home loans accounted for 34 percent of gross lending while in the second quarter of 1996 they were at their lowest level of around 25 percent.

The Council of Mortgage Lenders has yet to produce figures for the second quarter but said fixed rate lending accounted for 30 percent of the value of gross mortgage lending in the first quarter, compared with 21 percent in the final quarter of 1996.

"We saw a definite tendency towards fixed rate mortgages in the run-up to the election and clearly in the climate of expectations of higher interest rates, that's likely have continued," said Sue Anderson, the CML's head of external affairs. "At the moment all eyes are on fixed rates."
"In the U.S. the tradition has always been for fixed rate mortgages and people are now going for variable rate but over here it's the other way round.

The picture was similar at the Nationwide, Britain's biggest building society. "We're not seeing quite as much as 45 percent in fixed rate but it is quite close to that -- the discrepancy is perhaps because we're offering some very attractive variable rates at the moment," a Nationwide spokesman said.
He said the Nationwide was offering floating rate mortgages at 7.85 percent, compared with 8.2 percent by some of the major banks.

"We're seeing interest in mortgages fixed for five years, three years and one year -- in that order," he said. He said the Nationwide was offering mortgages fixed for the first five years at 7.59 percent for new borrowers and 7.49 percent for existing customers who wanted to take out a new mortgage.

The Halifax's Nicholson said the bank was seeing interest evenly spread between two, three and five year fixed rates. Its five year fixed rates range from 7.60 percent for existing borrowers and 7.95 percent for new customers borrowing 95 percent of the purchase price.
The current inversion in the British yield curve, whereby short term interest rates are much higher than long term ones, is also increasing the attractions of fixed rate mortgages.
"Fixed rates are below standard rates at the moment," said Nicholson. "The view is that base rates will rise further in the next 12 to 18 months and then potentially start to fall," he said.
But mortgage lenders are keen to point out that the housing market is not showing signs of overheating even if house prices are picking up in some areas such as the south east.
Housing market transactions are relatively steady at around 100,000 per month compared with double that at the top of the market in 1988.

There also hopes of another major difference from the last upswing in the property cycle -- that official interest rates are only around one percentage point from their peak. This would leave mortgages at a top level of just over 9.2 percent compared with their average over the past 20 years of 11.25 percent.
Overall around 80 percent of existing British mortgages are on a variable rate basis so the authorities still have scope to influence consumer demand by increasing interest rates.
But if the current trend to fixed rate mortgages continues, this position could change.
"If this pattern intensifies it will ultimately blunt the interest rate instrument, as some borrowers seek to by-pass rises in interest rates," said HSBC UK economist Jonathan Loynes.
--Cheryl Juckes, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5109
